https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: This mall was a symbol for San Francisco’s ‘doom loop’. Now it could become a datacenter project
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Developers propose turning San Francisco Centre into not a server-based facility, but a ‘community-based AI exhibit’

Downtown San Francisco has shown signs of revival since being battered by the Covid pandemic, which led to what many called a “doom loop” of vacant buildings, a worsening homelessness crisis and dwindling public transit. But one highly visible reminder of the city’s struggle to recover remains: the San Francisco Centre mall, which sits at the heart of these urban renewal efforts and has been conspicuously boarded up since January of this year.

A number of ideas have been floated for the mall’s reopening, including a multi-level sports complex, housing and more traditional retail uses. But now, another potential plan has emerged: the shuttered mall is being considered for an AI datacenter project, the San Francisco Chronicle reported.

In emails uncovered by the Chronicle, Maryland-based development firm KG Growth Partners asked San Francisco officials in June about datacenter permits on behalf of an unidentified potential buyer. Jared Krieger, the chief executive of KG Growth Partners, confirmed the Chronicle report, but said the firm had not yet applied for permits, “as we do not know if our client has won the bid to purchase”.

He stressed that the proposed project would not be a “traditional server-based datacenter” but instead a “cohesive, community-based AI exhibit”.

The Chronicle reported this “exhibit” includes plans to turn the 350,000 sq ft property formerly leased by Bloomingdale’s into an “AI-controlled living space” with a rooftop garden. Krieger clarified by email that these plans for a “living space” do not include actual residences. Instead he described the proposed project as “a living exhibit of how AI technology can interact with community and public spaces”, in which significant portions of the building would remain public facing. He said the project would include, “culture, design, retail, sports, and education spaces, along with a rooftop park”.

“As for concerns about foot traffic, this project is specifically designed to support the city’s vision,” he said. “By dedicating the majority of the space to public use, culture and retail, we are creating a destination that invites people downtown every day, directly supporting local businesses.”

Such a project may not have a straightforward path to approval. Backlash to datacenters has been on the rise across the US, and San Francisco – despite being the center of the AI boom – is no different. In response to growing concerns, Mayor Daniel Lurie signed a measure last week putting a moratorium on datacenter development in San Francisco for 45 days to allow the planning department time to research impacts of datacenters on communities where they are built. Lurie’s office did not respond to requests for comment regarding the Chronicle report. It is unclear how the potential downtown datacenter might be affected by this moratorium, as Krieger said it was “fundamentally different from a conventional datacenter”.

“We are proposing a regenerative urban energy center that recycles power and water, providing a clean energy supply and public benefits, rather than a sealed box that merely consumes from the grid,” he said.

Business owners downtown have long complained about the mall’s plight affecting the neighborhood ecosystem. The AI boom has brought money back to the Bay Area, and while the retail market in San Francisco at large has shown signs of recovery, businesses in the shadow of the shuttered mall say they aren’t seeing those effects.

Helen Nasser, who has owned SF Deli & Wine, a convenience store on the same block as the San Francisco Centre mall, for nearly 30 years, said she had watched a number of nearby stores close since the pandemic, and estimates business at her deli has plunged at least 60% since the mall closed.

“I’m the last man standing,” she said. “I need the mall to come back or I’m not going to survive.”

Nasser started the deli with her husband, who died 20 years ago, and said she has tried everything – including repeatedly emailing the mayor’s office for help – to keep her business afloat. She was shocked at potential plans to open a datacenter in the mall building, saying it is the “worst thing [Lurie] could do for the neighborhood”.

“We need the city to give back to the people – we need to utilize that space as somewhere families can go, where kids can go, and create something that brings foot traffic to the small businesses in the area,” she said. “If you put a datacenter there, you are going to kill us.”

https://www.theguardian.com/culture/2026.title: The little-known friendship between Nina Simone and Langston Hughes
https://www.theguardian.com/culture/2026.text:
A new book charts how a 1949 meeting between the renowned poet and the legendary musician, then a 16-year-old girl, sparked enduring ties and fruitful collaboration

In 1949, the poet and writer Langston Hughes was already a towering figure – he toured the country reading his poems and lecturing, drawing crowds that filled auditoriums. That year, at a lecture in Asheville, North Carolina, Hughes met a 16-year-old girl, Eunice Waymon, who would go on to make history in her own right using her stage name, Nina Simone.

Hughes and Simone became friends and collaborators, working together on songs such as Backlash Blues, which soundtracked what was then a nascent Black Power movement. The song influenced Kwame Ture, the activist and Black revolutionary who was then known as Stokely Carmichael, who popularized the phrase “Black power”.

“Nina Simone refined the strategies of resistance Langston Hughes pioneered during the Harlem Renaissance to create the soundtrack to the civil rights movement and inaugurate the birth of Black Power,” writes W Jason Miller, author of Don’t Let Me Be Misunderstood: Nina Simone, Langston Hughes, and the Birth of Black Power, a new book that explores the previously underacknowledged relationship between Hughes and Simone.

Using new first-hand accounts and archives, Miller, a distinguished professor of English at North Carolina State University, writes a history of the friendship between two American heavyweights. The Guardian spoke to Miller about Langston Hughes, Nina Simone and their relationship.

How did you settle on writing about Langston Hughes and Nina Simone’s relationship?

I’ve been a Langston Hughes scholar for about 22 years. At a book event in Raleigh, I told the audience that Hughes was approached by a singer to write the liner notes for her album. And Langston Hughes’ response was, “Why, Nina, I’d be happy to.”

The audience gasped at the thought of their Nina Simone, North Carolina icon, being in connection with Langston Hughes. I knew immediately that I had to find out everything about these two. I found one single sentence that even mentioned Nina Simone in seven biographies about Hughes.

For the last six years, I tracked down every letter they exchanged, every time they were together and located one of Nina’s roommates, a woman who, at 91 years old, remembered the day that Langston Hughes came to their high school and first met Nina.

I don’t think that either Hughes or Simone receive as much credit as they should for their role in the Black Power movement. Can you talk a bit about that?

Langston Hughes is often introduced as a figure of the Harlem Renaissance of the 1920s, of which he was of course a leading figure. But Hughes died in May of 1967 – less than 11 months before Dr King’s assassination. He was active, involved and productive up until the very end.

In terms of Nina Simone, her oeuvre and her musical career were wide and far-reaching. When folks think about the civil rights movement and reduce it to nonviolence, they miss Nina’s key role. If Nina were a figure of the civil rights movement leadership, she’s more like [Kwame Ture] than she is like Malcolm X or Martin Luther King. She’s a fiery young figure that can get overlooked by people that don’t know, but the people that latch on to her know her iconic songs and her protest music. Their ability together created the soundtrack to the civil rights movement.

Langston Hughes really wanted to have a hit song written. He’d been trying since 1949 to break through in music. He had this desire to have Nina Simone sing one of his songs. The last poem that Hughes ever sent out for publication was called Backlash Blues. It’s the poem he gave to Nina to sing that became her iconic song.

This book is a biography of their friendship, which involves strategies for how two figures go through the practice of mentoring, building a relationship and collaborating. Nina sat in the third row at the 1960 Newport jazz festival while Hughes led a blues session in which he was directing Muddy Waters and John Lee Hooker for two and a half hours. Nina saw Hughes not just as an important cultural icon, she recognized him as a music lover that she could trust.

Leonard Bernstein and Walt Disney are generally more associated with making classical music accessible to a wider audience. But you argue that Simone did something similar with her interpolation of Bach in Love Me or Leave Me and a few other pieces.

Nina Simone grows up in Tryon, is educated in Asheville, North Carolina, with the goal of becoming a classical pianist. Her icon is Hazel Scott and her favorite musician of all time was Bach. What she was able to do in the very end of her career is combine popular music with classical music. She hides classical music inside of these popular songs. Unconsciously, audience members that listened to the vinyl or saw her in concert were being exposed to classical music.

For her first concert at Carnegie Hall, Andy Stroud, her manager husband, puts up a great deal of money, hires a big promoter, and they’re worried about being able to sell out. The first half of that entire concert is filled with classical instrumental music, not her singing. Langston Hughes had written promotional materials, so posters and newspaper ads had blurbs of support from Hughes.

What about their upbringing as southerners influenced their relationship and their wider reputations?

Nina Simone’s education in western North Carolina shapes her a great deal. She starts playing in the church. That area of the country gives us the incredible song Sinner Man, one she heard and performed. In late 1965, at the prompting of Langston Hughes, she records it, and it becomes a way to retell history. We’re not just thinking about God, the devil and the sinner. We’re thinking about student ambassadors who are trying to fight for change, white Klan members and the role of prayer in the civil rights movement.

Hughes’ grandmother spent time here in North Carolina with the Lumbee people. Right before he met Nina Simone, Langston Hughes gave a newspaper interview where he talked about his grandmother being part Lumbee and being part of the North Carolina tradition.

Hughes was condemned for his leftist politics and Simone faced similar condemnation. Do you think that their relationship informed their ability to use art to convey their political messages?

Langston Hughes not only recognized the talent that Nina Simone had, he not only had this desire to have his music performed, and he not only had a genuine interest in supporting the next generation, but he recognized that she could use the same strategies he had pioneered in the Harlem Renaissance. If you’re an academic, we call this signifying. If you’re a high school teacher, we call it allusion. But all people today know this as sampling.

Nina learned she could sample old music and update it. When she sang songs like Tomorrow Is My Turn, she turned a love song into a statement that tomorrow I’m going to get a chance. When she took songs like Go to Hell, Nina writes a new last verse. She says: we are in hell.

She brought this to her work in Sinner Man, especially. Nina activated those characters by thinking about Jimmy Lee Jackson and what started the march from Selma to Montgomery. When Nina used strategies to seem to be talking about something and slip it in, that’s when she was tuning her soul to the wavelength of Langston Hughes.

It starts with Langston Hughes’ spirit. The list of people he welcomed into his orbit and deliberately mentored is unbelievable. It includes Gwendolyn Brooks, Margaret Walker and he was very supportive of Amiri Baraka. I met a woman in Oxford, North Carolina – Mary “Pee Wee” Lindsay. She talked about meeting Hughes in the early 1950s, walking up to him with a couple pages of poems. She said that Hughes sat down with her for 30 minutes and went through those poems, even though she had no international-level talent, never published a book.

Simone and Hughes connected because, in so many ways, they were moving in the same direction. When Langston Hughes dies in 1967, Nina has Backlash Blues ready, but she hasn’t recorded or released it. After he dies, she writes a new verse. She includes their relationship. That leads her to understand one of Hughes’ key lessons, which is how to incorporate great people into music and art. One year later, she recognizes Martin Luther King’s assassination. Nina composed and thought of the song To Be Young, Gifted and Black in 1969. Hughes’ relationship sent her on this course of making music like Backlash Blues, Why the King of Love Is Dead, To Be Young, Gifted and Black that would stand as symbols of these great people.

https://www.theguardian.com/tv-and-radio.title: ‘It was so satisfying when I threw a rock through the screen’: the people sick of being spied on by their smart TV
https://www.theguardian.com/tv-and-radio.text:
Is your television listening to every conversation? Filling your home with highly invasive ads? Some viewers have had enough of tech violating their privacy

Some may accuse Dan of being a luddite, but his master’s degree in computer science and decades of experience in telecommunications would suggest otherwise. “The tech is not intimidating,” he explains, “just increasingly enshittified.”

The first smart TVs entered the market in the late 2000s, when companies introduced operating systems, media players and apps to screens that were becoming wider and thinner. In recent years, the luxury status of smart TVs has waned and increasingly affordable options are widely available. Tom Parsons, TV and audiovisual editor at the electronics magazine What Hi-Fi?, explains that these cheaper models can struggle under more advanced features. “They’re not necessarily super-fast and responsive out of the box,” he says. “And then two, three, four years down the line, they can end up slowing down quite a lot under the weight of all that processing.”

Dan is just one of a growing number of tech-savvy watchers wishing their TVs weren’t so smart. Erin McQuiston and Matthew Schroyer, a couple from Connecticut, share his smart-screen scepticism.

“I don’t think we’ve ever used [our TV] as anything other than just a giant display,” says McQuiston. “There was a period where we were running it through an Xbox. And that was a constant battle because that was constantly being updated and patched and then you’d have to redownload all the apps for it.”

Meanwhile, Schroyer says his job as a software engineer has influenced his decision to “intentionally keep it very dumb” by keeping their TV disconnected from the internet. “A rule of the house is: don’t give things the wifi password,” he says. “It concerns me that folks increasingly have to be IT experts to get the bare minimum enjoyable experience out of this stuff.”

Instead, the 41-year-old connects his screen to an Apple TV box as a streaming workaround, and cites privacy as well as “highly invasive” advertisements for doing so. “Our living room is not a billboard for sale,” he says.

When asked how the couple might cope in a future where TVs may have mandatory internet, McQuiston says her husband is “handy enough to break every terms of service known to man and get in there and unsolder something to manually disconnect it”.

For Helen Northmore, a 51-year-old from Wales who works in AI delivery for the UK Health Security Agency, privacy is also a worry. Her grudge against smart screens began four years ago, when her faithful dumb TV broke without warning and she had to quickly find a replacement.

“We had already decided that we didn’t want the smart functionality, but it became really clear that it was very hard to find one that didn’t have any,” she says. Northmore, whose partner works in cybersecurity, says the couple wanted to “keep control” over their devices, which cost them a premium. “We were willing to pay more. One of the boundaries in how we live our lives is we want to minimise the smart element. We don’t have smart speakers. We don’t enable or connect to the internet.”

Today, she watches entertainment through a Sky box connected to her dumb TV, and dreads that when her current telly breaks there won’t be any option but to get a smart model and offer up her data.

More consumers are becoming worried about how their information is being used by manufacturers. “There are increasing privacy concerns around to what degree TVs are essentially scraping your data,” says Parsons. “TVs these days are full of sensors, including microphones, and that can make people nervous.”

But according to Parsons, despite interest in “dumber” models from some buyers, most shoppers want their TVs to be catch-all entertainment systems. The result is that the dumb TV market is almost nonexistent. “You can buy cheap monitors for signage,” he says, “but from a features point of view, you wouldn’t get the same performance that you would from a consumer TV.”

Paul, a public servant from Australia, knows just how hard finding a traditional TV can be. “When my last telly – a glorious 32-inch dumb TV – died recently, aged approximately 10 years old, I spent about three weeks scouring the city looking for something comparable. What I found is that they do not exist any more.”

After much searching, Paul discovered a single 40-inch TV without any smart functionality in the back of a shop. “It had zero ways to connect to the internet – just a couple of plugs on the back for making it work with the aerial on the roof and my VHS player, and that was it.” He remembers that it “was very dusty and cost about 200 dollars. Naturally, we fell instantly in love.”

“My friends all laugh at it when they come over,” he admits, “but secretly I know the joke is on them. My little telly doesn’t spy on me, and has a DVD player built in.”

The punchline may eventually land on Paul, however. In September, the Australian government launched a consultation into the future of the country’s free-to-air broadcasting, asking citizens for feedback on how TV should be accessed. One of the proposed scenarios would see traditional broadcast services cut in favour of streaming services and video on-demand apps.

In the same month, the UK government released a media green paper outlining its plan to fully move away from digital terrestrial television to services provided over a broadband connection by 2034 at the earliest. Such a situation would mean viewers having to rely on broadcaster apps and streaming services.

If a similar fate befell North America, James certainly wouldn’t care. He is originally from the US but now lives in British Columbia, Canada, and says traditional broadcast TV is “dead to him” and that he prefers to watch shows on streaming services or on YouTube. For the father and husband, privacy is a top priority.

“No one expects an end-user licence agreement to include giving up autonomy,” he says. “Having my TV listen to any conversation and use that for monetary or any form of gain is above and beyond expectations on the loss of privacy.”

In September, the YouTube channel Gamers Nexus released a two-hour investigation into LG Electronics’ smart televisions, saying that the devices record audio – even when they are offline or powered down. The South Korean company denied the allegations. In the fallout, some have taken measures to modify their smart TVs, regardless of brand or model. Some videos online show users replacing motherboards, cutting out Bluetooth and wifi modules and removing microphones from their TV remote controls.

Amid the controversy, James read online advice that modifying a TV remote microphone was a simple procedure. So he surgically removed the sensor himself. “Removing the mic was literally as easy as using a [craft] knife to scrape it off the top,” he says, “and the remote continued to work fine.”

James’s willingness to dissect his tech comes from fears for his children. “My kids are not teenagers and they have no agency to protect their private information,” he says. “Someone listening in on a TV gets to find out about my daughter’s first period without her knowing. And that is a level of invasion no one should have without explicit consent.”

Frustration and controversies have sparked a DIY interest in opening up and neutering the black rectangles in our living rooms. Though the desire in the first place may lead consumers to ask themselves an important question: have our TVs become too smart for their own good?

Gutting any piece of electronic equipment should be left to professionals. However, some may find that, for a complex problem, the simplest solutions are the most elegant. As Dan recalls: “It was enormously satisfying when I threw a rock through the screen.”

https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/oc.title: Tom Cruise’s Digger is a commercial flop – but also the perfect climate film for our time
https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/oc.text:
The movie follows Digger Rockwell, whose drilling triggers a vast iceberg that’s five times the size of Washington DC

Digger, the new Alejandro González Iñárritu film, is bombastic, misanthropic and an epic, critically savaged flop. It is also the near-perfect climate change film for our era.

Digger Rockwell, the eponymous protagonist played by Tom Cruise, is a bluntly caricatured Texas oilman blase about the environmental ruin of his drilling, even as it triggers a disastrous splitting of the Arctic ice sheet. This causes a vast iceberg, five times the size of Washington DC, to barrel towards Europe and threaten a devastating tsunami.

Much like this impending disaster and the real-world retreat of glaciers and coral reefs, though, the mere act of watching Digger has become a forlorn race against time. The box office failure has been resounding, and Digger’s time on the big screen has been brief.

Facing a predicted $245m loss – the lavishly made film took $8m in its first weekend in the US before dropping 60% for its second – Digger was yanked from more than 2,500 theatres across the US ahead of its third week. Scrambling to find a single cinema showing Digger, I had to resort to spending a Thursday lunchtime with just two other ticket-buying patrons at a major Manhattan venue.

The critical opprobrium and dismal ticket sales shouldn’t be a shock. Fans of Cruise are used to mass appeal movies of clean-cut heroism, not him aged, balding and dressed in a Stetson and cowboy boots and little else as he howls a confected Texan drawl in a dark climate satire.

The film also, as critics have pointed out, strays into a “glib and overblown” depiction of elite cowardice and cynicism when it comes to the climate crisis.

There are heavy-handed scenes of Digger eating endangered tuna in front of his aghast chief scientist Nirav Ganesh (a harried Riz Ahmed) and of sneering indifference from a US president (played dyspeptically by John Goodman) when confronted by the looming catastrophe.

“You know what, this isn’t my problem,” the president says when confronted with ecological and societal doom. A farcically bellicose, Pete Hegseth-like general dismisses the iceberg as a snow cone and advises the president to “blow that frozen cunt up” with nuclear weapons.

At one point, Digger and Ganesh sit in a room gazing at flickering flames, as if they are in hell. It’s not a cheery message, but it is a franker one than the other, scarce attempts to depict the climate crisis on screen. Perhaps we are actually in hell, the movie suggests, and the evil oil tycoons aren’t the only ones to blame for that.

It is cathartic to see Ganesh berate Digger for being guilty of the “most heinous act of all time” by knowing, as oil companies did in reality for decades, of the consequences of global heating but then fatally obscuring this knowledge in order to rake in more cash. But Digger goes further than just unmasking a single villain.

Don’t Look Up, the 2021 climate allegory, frames the problem as frantic scientists being ignored as an asteroid heads towards Earth. Digger’s message is a more sinister but uncomfortably accurate one – that we all know of the cataclysm we are inflicting upon current and future generations but have largely acquiesced to it.

“Let’s cut the bullshit, you love oil,” as Digger tells enraged European lawmakers, all dressed in muted beige and grey, in a lengthy rant. “You want to bask in your unsustainable lives.”

The oil companies may have lied and bought off politicians, but, in the wealthy west at least, we have all been complicit by failing to punish leaders for this and we remain willing customers for the poison of fossil fuels, even as they choke, drown and fry us.

Any sort of lifestyle change – eating less meat, flying less, switching to a car that doesn’t have a petrol pump on hand at each corner – is too much hassle for most of us even as we face the biggest threat to menace humanity. There are always, as Digger points out to the Eurocrats, phones to be charged, TikToks to watch. In holding up a mirror to this, Digger might not be the climate film we want. But it may be the one we need.

It’s striking that the possible end of a habitable planet has spawned comparatively little art with only vague nods, if at all, to our culpability. Among movies, there was Waterworld, another flop where Kevin Costner had to drink his own urine on a world flooded by the melted ice caps, and The Day After Tomorrow, where the melting ice causes a storm that plunges society into a new ice age.

Musically, the best of a meagre bunch is perhaps Smash Mouth’s 1999 hit song All Star which includes a lament of thinning ice and the line “my world’s on fire, how ‘bout yours?” The climate crisis may seem too overwhelming and gloomy to depict, but also, maybe we have so closeted and normalized our guilt that it feels shameful to bring it out into the light to be examined in public.

Digger forces us to not look away, even as we squirm at what we’ve done. “This film is a disaster movie,” Iñárritu has said. “But the disaster is us.”

The film is too nihilistic about our lack of response – Digger condemns clean energy as useless and his half-sister Emma (played by a squandered Sandra Hüller) makes endeavors in renewables that are dismissively mocked. Yet in real life the industry is growing explosively. We have everything we need to confront the climate crisis, after all, bar the necessary willpower.

Digger won’t be the last climate film. Later this year, A Statement, a dramatization of a real-life 1980 meeting of experts on what to do about global warming starring Paul Rudd and Paul Giamatti, will be released.

But Digger was the last Warner Bros’s theatrical release before it was purchased by Paramount Skydance and the Ellisons. Its commercial failure, along with the ideological leanings of the movie studio overlords, may deter further attempts to give us unvarnished tales of the climate crisis. That would be a huge, iceberg-sized mistake.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: DIY repair clubs are helping Americans save money and fight big tech
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
US community repair clinics teach people how to fix their belongings, pushing back against throwaway culture

On a recent Monday night, a volunteer-run workspace bustled with dozens of fixers in Brooklyn, New York. Some tinkered with sewing machines while others soldered circuit boards at a workbench. Caleb Young, a co-founder of the Brooklyn Spark space, fit a DIY suction device on to the handle of a Dyson vacuum cleaner.

“It’s in our culture to throw things away, but sometimes the fix is easier than you’d think,” Young said.

The Fixit Clinic is open every Monday night to walk-ins. Anyone with a broken item they’d like to fix – from torn clothes to malfunctioning electronic devices – can drop by during open hours and get the repair help and tools they need. It’s a way for people to push back against tech companies, making their phones and gadgets deliberately unrepairable so they buy newer devices while creating large amounts of e-waste. The clinics also foster community: once people learn to repair their possessions, many get addicted and like helping others, Young said.

“We like to tell them, ‘Why not take a few seconds to try and open something up?’” he said. “It’s broken anyway.”

The Brooklyn clinic is part of a nationwide network offering community repair. Peter Mui, who founded the first Fixit Clinic in Berkeley, California, in 2009, said that he has seen the number of clinics explode during the past few years; at least 2,000 have been hosted across the country. “We’re offering these workshops in libraries, at colleges and in public spaces where fixers and community members can come together,” Mui said.

Similar, unaffiliated clinics have seen success, too. The community-run Repair cafe, originally founded in Amsterdam, now has about 250 US locations. Neighborhood repair events at local community centers are also popping up around the country.

Policy proposals have even matched this grassroots demand. Since 2012, 24 states have successfully passed some form of right-to-repair legislation, mandating that manufacturers make their products repair-friendly instead of destined for the landfill. This year, 57 right-to-repair bills have been introduced in 22 states that would make machines such as phones, wheelchairs and construction equipment easier to repair. Members of Congress have also introduced a bipartisan federal automotive right-to-repair bill, called the Repair Act, but it has yet to be brought to a full House vote.

Mui attributes the growing interest to people questioning the environmental and economic costs of our consumer culture. “So much of our capitalist system is tied up in our endless consumption,” he said. “But if we come together to take agency and empowerment over the things we own, we can build a more sustainable future.”

The first modern right-to-repair state law was passed in 2012, when Massachusetts granted car owners the right to fix their cars at independent service shops. Congress passed a bill in 2014 that legalized “phone unlocking”, which allowed consumers to change their cell service carrier without buying a new phone. Farmers and states have also filed lawsuits against the agricultural equipment manufacturer John Deere over repair restrictions to their equipment, resulting in settlements with the company.

Right to repair reached a new level of public consciousness in 2024 when customers across the country were upset over broken McFlurry machines. The Digital Millennium Copyright Act (DMCA) protected the software on these machines, meaning only their manufacturer, Taylor, could fix them. After petitions from consumers and consumer advocacy groups, the US copyright office granted a copyright exemption that would allow third-party repairs on McFlurry machines.

Nathan Proctor, the senior director of the Right to Repair campaign at the Public Interest Research Group, said that corporations’ responses to right-to-repair laws have ranged from compliance to active resistance. For example, Apple has gradually made some parts and manuals available for repair, while the automotive industry has fought back against right-to-repair laws. “Some companies are hostile and refuse to provide repair materials, while others have made national policies to sell spare parts,” he said.

But the growing grassroots movement of community repair brings Proctor hope. “We need to both change the law and build out a culture of repair,” Proctor said. “To see these community events start up with no institutional backing – that’s a signal that something about repair is clicking with people.”

At San Jose State University in California, the Fixit Clinic student organization was recently voted the most influential club on campus. The student-led group holds monthly clinics for fellow students and community members at libraries around the city. “We like to tell people, ‘If you can get it through the door, we can fix it for you,’” said club president Lily Andrews.

Since the chapter was founded in 2024, the club has hosted on-campus and off-campus workshops to teach middle schoolers, college students and community members skills including sewing and soldering metals. Andrews, a college junior studying mechanical engineering, said that hosting these clinics has offered her hands-on practice that goes beyond the theories she is learning in the classroom. “When I open things up, I get to really see how they’re made, and see how the machinery components interact,” she said.

Andrews said she has learned how many of our products are made to discourage repair. “All these nuts, bolts and screws make it intimidating to take things apart,” she said.

Mui, the founder of the first Fixit Clinic, said that this is the next step in the clinics’ mission: launching more events in partnership with colleges and universities to educate the next generation of designers and engineers. “I’m focused on asking, ‘How do we train students to rethink the whole system?’” he said.

Andrews says that her experience leading the club has inspired her to pave a different path forward. “Fixing and repairing isn’t just an engineering skill; it’s a skill that everyone should have,” she said. “I want to keep applying what I’ve learned in my work so that we can keep items from landing in the landfill, help the environment and reduce waste.”

https://www.theguardian.com/culture/2026.title: RJ Mitte obituary
https://www.theguardian.com/culture/2026.text:
Film and TV actor with cerebral palsy who played Walter White Jr in Breaking Bad and was a staunch disability rights campaigner

The actor RJ Mitte was a natural choice to play Walter White Jr, the son of Walter White (Bryan Cranston), the high school chemistry teacher turned meth dealer, in the television series Breaking Bad (2008-13), generally regarded as one of the greatest shows of the streaming era.

Walt Jr, also known as Flynn, was modelled by the show’s creator, Vince Gilligan, on the son of a friend who had cerebral palsy. Mitte had been diagnosed with cerebral palsy as an infant, and told the Guardian in 2015 that when he read the character summary he thought it “pretty much described me. ‘Dark hair, big eyebrows, cerebral palsy … ’ I was, like, ‘I have this covered.’”

He actually had to overplay the extent of his disability for the part (for example, depending on crutches that he did not need), and from the start his was a key role. Care for Flynn was part of the White family’s financial bind, but it was the boy’s changing relationship to his dad that became the audience’s window into Walt Sr’s progression into vicious gangster. Mitte grew alongside his character. “We watched him grow into a really fine actor ... that promise and potential now is a real loss,” said Cranston of his co-star.

His success as an actor helped Mitte, who has taken his own life aged 34, become a prominent activist for disabled people, working with the United Cerebral Palsy organisation and the Shriners Children’s hospital network. He did not believe cerebral palsy was a hindrance to him. “You develop a different look at how the world sees you and how you see the world,” he said. “I think it’s an asset.” And from early in his life he was determined to make it one.

I met RJ at the 2016 Paralympics Games in Rio, where I was a commentator for wheelchair basketball for the host broadcaster and he was working for the British TV station Channel 4. He was an amazing combination of intense focus and almost off-the-wall randomness, fuelled by incredible energy and, of course, a killer smile and laugh.

He was born, not breathing, via emergency caesarean section, in Jackson, Mississippi, and suffered brain damage during the delivery. Soon afterwards he was adopted by Dyna (nee Carriere) and RF Mitte Jr, and named Roy Frank Mitte III, later known as RJ (“Roy Junior”). Two months later, the couple split up, and Dyna raised her son alone. At three, RJ was diagnosed with cerebral palsy, and his legs were put in casts for six months, a process that would continue through his therapy in order to straighten his feet.

When RJ was 11, his younger sister, Lacianne (Lacey), was born, but a few weeks afterwards his mother was paralysed in a car accident. RJ helped financially by cutting lawns, doing odd jobs and collecting bottles for refunds.

He was as much father as brother to Lacey, who, in 2006, still an infant, was spotted in a Houston park by a talent scout who offered to represent her. The family moved to Los Angeles, where her agency also arranged acting lessons for RJ. He got small parts in Everyone Hates Chris and in Hannah Montana, before being hired for Breaking Bad, which debuted in January 2008, when he was 15. It ran for five seasons and won six Emmy awards, including in 2014 the prize for best ensemble cast.

In 2013, Mitte won the Screen Actors Guild’s Harold Russell award, given in recognition of those “who advance the accurate portrayal and employment of people with disabilities”. “Hollywood has always portrayed disability as a weakness, something you have to overcome,” Mitte said. “To me it’s the complete opposite ... it’s a personal challenge to grow and explore.”

After Breaking Bad, Mitte appeared on TV in an episode of Vegas (2013) and then a full season in Switched at Birth (2014), as a wheelchair user, the love interest for the deaf girl Daphne, one of the “switched” characters of the title.

His film work was largely with independents, in a number of horror and crime films, and others where his cerebral palsy was a part of the story. Who’s Driving Doug (2016) is a road movie written by a man with muscular dystrophy. Mitte was particularly good in the Australian Standing Up for Sunny (2019), in which he played a disabled man who is dragged into an attempt to make a hesitant standup comic more confident. Critics praised the comic timing between Mitte and Philippa Northeast, as the comedienne.

In Triumph (2021), Mitte played a bullied student with cerebral palsy who takes up wrestling to prove himself in high school. On TV he played the Mind Master in 2022 in the successful part-animated series The Guardians of Justice. Perhaps his most impressive film was the poorly distributed All the Little Things We Kill (2019), in which a college professor holds a classroom hostage in order to get a ban on semi-automatic weapons passed.

Earlier this year, in the film Talking to Strangers, he played a loner with cerebral palsy who opens his tightly structured world to an exuberant woman, who later tells him that she plans to take her own life. One Eye Open was scheduled for release in the week of Mitte’s death; another film, Cassi, has been finished and awaits its release date.

In 2025, Mitte announced his engagement to his long-term girlfriend Kennedy Suarez. He is survived by his mother and sister.
